blocks.text: It is proved that שפיפון sephiphon, Gen. XLIX, 17, is the cerastes and the haemorrhous.

At Gen. XLIX, 17, I cannot at all understand why the Greeks rendered שפיפון sephiphon as ἐγκαθήμενον [enkathēmenon], and the Samaritans as ࠊࠌࠉࠍ · lying in ambush. But I know that others hold, much more correctly, that שפיפון is a kind of serpent. For this is openly proclaimed by the words of Jacob, which run thus: DAN shall be a serpent by the way, a שפיפון sephiphon by the path, that bites the horse's heels, so that his rider falls backward. Thus it is quite certain that the sesiphon is a serpent. Only the species is in doubt. The Hebrews, indeed, concern themselves solely with the origin of the word. Aben Ezra derives it from the verb שוף, to bruise, because it was said to the serpent in Gen. III, 15. אתה תשופנו עקב, You shall bruise his heel. Kimchi derives it from the verb שפה, which also has the meaning to bruise in Iob. XXXIII, 21. So שפיפון would be formed from שפה with the second radical doubled, as הגיגי from הגה. But Selomo and Pomarius prefer to derive it from נשף, to blow, or to hiss. This is what the Hebrews say on the origin of the word; on its proper meaning, οὐδὲ γρύ [oude gry]. If you consult others, however, their very diversity will leave you doubtful and uncertain. Jonathan explains it as רישי חיוין, the chief of serpents; Onkelos as פתנה, an asp; the Jerusalem Targum and the Syriac as ܡܥܪܘܢܐ, a basilisk; both Arabic versions as معرون [maʿrūn], explaining the unknown by the more unknown; Jerome as cerastes; Junius as acontias; Schindler, under ארח, as viper; Castalio and the Italian, French and English versions as snake.

In this darkness we borrow some light from the Arabs, among whom سف sipphon, or supphon, is a serpent marked with white and black. Alcamus: السف الارقم من الحيات [al-siff al-arqam min al-ḥayyāt], Sipphon (or supphon) is, among serpents, the one called [col. 417] arkamo (variegated). And elsewhere: الارقم اخبث الحيات واطلبها للناس او ما فيه سواد وبياض [al-arqam akhbath al-ḥayyāt wa-aṭlabuhā li-l-nās aw mā fīhi sawād wa-bayāḍ], Arkamo, the most pernicious of serpents and the most hostile to man; or one that is partly black, partly white. Hence there is a weighty conjecture that the sipphon is the haemorrhous and haemorrhois, of which Aëtius says: These animals are sandy in colour, etc. But over the body they are variegated with black and white marks. Likewise Avicenna ^{a)}: ذكرت القدما ان هاتين الحيتين رمليتا الابدان وعلي ابدانها نقط سود وبيض [dhakarat al-qudamā an hātayn al-ḥayyatayn ramliyyatā al-abdān wa-ʿalī abdānihā nuqaṭ sūd wa-bīḍ] The ancients report that these serpents have sandy bodies, and that these are sprinkled with [III, 206] black and white spots. So if שפיפון sephiphon is explained from Arabic usage, it will seem to be the haemorrhois, a species of viper whose bite draws out blood, so that whatever life there is is summoned out through the blood, as we read in Solinus.

Yet the Vulgate version, which renders it cerastes, greatly appeals to me, because the nature of the cerastes seems plainly expressed in Jacob's words, "Dan shall be a serpent by the way, שפיפון עלי ארח, a sephiphon by the path"; or, as others render it, on the wheel-track. For that is where the cerastes lurks, as Nicander says in the Theriaca, line 262.
— — — ἐν δ᾽ ἀμάθοισιν Ἠ καὶ ἁματροχιῇσι παρὰ στίβον· — — [en d᾽ amathoisin ē kai hamatrochiēsi para stibon]

In the sand, or even in the wheel-ruts beside the road, so as to lie in wait for travellers from there. And Jacob adds that the sephiphon bites the horse's heels so that the rider falls backward, namely when the horse stumbles as the poison begins to creep into its hocks. For the same Nicander relates that the force of the evil shows itself chiefly in the hollows of the knees and in the groin:

Διπλοῖς δ᾽ ἐν βουβῶσιν, καὶ ἰγνύσιν ἀσκελὲς αὐτὸς Μόχθος ἐπιτρέφεται· — — — [Diplois d᾽ en boubōsin, kai ignysin askeles autos Mochthos epitrephetai] Soon heavy suffering afflicts the groin, and pain sharply presses both knee-hollows. — — —

And this bite is deadly not only to men but also to beasts. For Callias in Aelian, book 16, chapter 28, says: Τοὺς κεράστας ὄφεις δεινοὺς εἶναι τὸ δῆγμα, ἀναιρεῖν γὰρ τὰ ζῶα ἄλογα, καὶ ἀνθρώπους· [Tous kerastas opheis deinous einai to dēgma, anairein gar ta zōa aloga, kai anthrōpous] The cerastes serpents are dangerous in their bite, and kill both beasts and men. What is most serious is that the ambush of the cerastes is not easily avoided: since it is the colour of the sand, it is trodden on by the unwary, whom it bites in return. Diodorus, book 3 ^{b)}: Τὴν δὲ χρόαν ἄμμῳ παραπλησίαν ἔχουσι· διόπερ ἐξωμοιωμένων αὐτῶν κατὰ τὴν πρόσοψιν τοῖς ὑποκειμένοις ἐδάφεσι, ὀλίγοι μὲν ἐπιγινώσκουσιν· οἱ πολλοὶ δ᾽ ἀγνοοῦντες πατοῦσι, καὶ κινδύνοις περιπίπτουσιν ἀπροσδοκήτοις. [Tēn de chroan ammō paraplēsian echousi; dioper exōmoiōmenōn autōn kata tēn prosopsin tois hypokeimenois edaphesi, oligoi men epiginōskousin; hoi polloi d᾽ agnoountes patousi, kai kindynois peripiptousin aprosdokētois.] They resemble sand in colour; therefore, since they are like the ground beneath them in colour, few recognize them, and most tread on them unawares and so fall into unforeseen dangers. Hence it came about that these serpents once entirely depopulated a part of Ethiopia bordering on Egypt, as Diodorus relates in the same place.
